225.title: Pauri 36, meaning: the realm of effort
225.hook: knowledge blazes; then comes the realm of effort, where beauty shapes mind and understanding (Japji 36)
225.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 36 describes Saram Khand, the third of the five realms, which Sikh teachers variously explain as the realm of effort, of humility, or of spiritual joy, where the mind itself is reshaped.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 36. Your line was giaan khandd: in the realm of knowledge, knowledge blazes. Did something new make you smile? Today, the next realm, and it's a workshop. Day two hundred twenty-five.

Watch someone learn the violin. The first month is painful for everyone in the house. Squeaks, scratches, a bow that won't sit straight. But something is happening that you can't hear yet. The fingertips are hardening. The ear is learning to catch a note that's slightly off. Six months in, the student hears music differently, not just plays it differently. The practice has been shaping the player all along. Anyone who has trained for anything, a sport, a language, a craft, knows this. You work on the thing, and the thing works on you. Pauri 36 calls the next realm a workshop where exactly that happens.
screen: `A MONTH OF SQUEAKS.` → `THE EAR IS LEARNING.` → `THE THING WORKS ON YOU.`

segments.voice: After knowledge blazes, the stanza turns: saram khandd kee baanee roop. The language of Saram Khand is beauty, is form. Then: tithai ghaarrat gharreeai bahut anoop. There, shaping is done, beyond compare. Gharreeai is the word for what a potter or a smith does, forming something by hand. And what gets shaped? Tithai gharreeai surat mat man budh. There, awareness, intellect, mind and understanding are shaped. Not clay. You. In the realm of knowledge, you saw how big creation is. In this realm, the seeing gets worked into who you are. And here's a small, honest admission in the middle of it: taa keeaa galaa katheeaa naa jaahi, je ko kahai pichhai pachhutaae. Its matters can't be told; whoever tries will be sorry afterward. Even Nanak refuses to over-describe it. Now, what does saram mean? Here, teachers honestly differ. Many translators read it as effort or striving, from an old word for labor, and that's the reading in today's title. Others hear saram as modesty or humility. That's the same word you met in Pauri 28, where modesty was the yogi's begging bowl. And some read it as spiritual joy. Sikh teachers often hold these together: the humble, beautiful work of being reshaped. Either way, the picture is a workshop. Knowledge showed you the size of things. Effort, patient and humble, lets that knowledge reshape the mind.
screen: `SARAM KHAND — THE LANGUAGE IS BEAUTY.` · `GHARREEAI — SHAPED, LIKE CLAY.` · `AWARENESS, MIND, UNDERSTANDING.` · `EFFORT, HUMILITY: READINGS DIFFER.` · then, large: `EFFORT SHAPES THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you'll do today with real effort, the kind you usually rush: washing a pan, writing a message, tying your shoes, listening to someone. Picture yourself doing it slowly and well, the way a craftsperson would. Then, for the rest of the sit, give the same care to your breath. Breathe in fully. Breathe out completely. Let each breath be well made, one at a time. The bell holds the time.
Saram Khand. The realm of effort, a workshop where beauty is the language and awareness, mind and understanding are shaped. The third of Japji's five realms.
Your line: effort shapes the mind. Today, do the small thing you chose with real care, start to finish, and notice how it shapes you back. Day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: Pauri 37, sound: karam khandd
226.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes the last two of the five realms, and its opening, karam khandd kee baanee jor, echoes the frame of the line before it about Saram Khand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saram Khand, the workshop. Your line was effort shapes the mind. Did you do one small thing with real care, start to finish? Today, the fourth realm, sound first. Day two hundred twenty-six.

Songwriters know a trick. You write a line, and later in the song you bring back its exact shape with one word changed, and the listener's ear lights up. The same frame, a new filling. It tells you: we've moved, but we're still in the same song. Yesterday's stanza gave us a frame: saram khandd kee baanee roop. The language of the realm of effort is beauty. Pauri 37 opens with that same frame, changes two words, and suddenly we're somewhere new. And one of the words it brings in is an old friend, the hammer from Pauri 33. Today, just listen for the echo.
screen: `THE SAME FRAME, A NEW WORD.` → `SARAM KHANDD KEE BAANEE ROOP.` → `LISTEN FOR THE ECHO.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 37: karam khandd kee baanee jor. Put it next to yesterday's: saram khandd kee baanee roop. Same frame. Saram becomes karam; roop becomes jor. Let's take the new words. Karam: grace, generosity, kindness freely given. It's a Persian word, and it's easy to confuse with karma, which means action and its results. Both appear in the Granth. Here, Sikh commentators generally read karam as grace. Karam khandd: the realm of grace. Kee baanee: its language, its mark. Jor: power, strength. The language of the realm of grace is power. Now remember Pauri 33, where jor hammered through every line with no beside it: no power to speak, no power to be silent, no power of our own. Here jor comes back, and there's no no. The power that wasn't ours is at home in the realm of grace. Then the second line: tithai hor na koee hor. Tithai: there. Hor: other, else. Na koee: not anyone. Hor again. There, no one else, no other at all. Hear how hor bookends the line, the way jor boxed in the lines of Pauri 33. The whole stanza has a strong, even beat; many hear it as the most majestic part of the Japji. Tomorrow we'll open who lives in this realm, and what lies beyond it. Today, listen to saram become karam, and jor come home.
screen: `SARAM BECOMES KARAM.` · `KARAM — GRACE, NOT KARMA.` · `JOR — POWER, AND NO NO THIS TIME.` · `TITHAI HOR NA KOEE HOR.` · then, large: `KARAM KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the first two lines aloud: karam khandd kee baanee jor, tithai hor na koee hor. Say them three times, with a strong, even beat. Then say yesterday's line once, saram khandd kee baanee roop, and today's once more, and hear the echo. Afterward, sit in silence. With each breath out, let yourself feel held by a strength that isn't yours to earn. Just rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 37. It opens in the realm of grace: karam khandd kee baanee jor, its language is power, and there is no one else, no other at all.
Your line: karam khandd, the realm of grace. Today, notice one good thing that came to you that you did nothing to earn. Day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: Pauri 37, meaning: grace and truth
227.hook: in the realm of grace dwell the mighty in spirit; in the realm of truth dwells the Formless, beholding all (Japji 37)
227.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes Karam Khand, the realm of grace, and Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless dwells, and ends with Nanak saying that describing it is as hard as steel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 37. Your line was karam khandd, the realm of grace. Did one unearned good thing come your way? Today, the grace realm opened, and the last realm of all. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Try this. Describe your mother's voice, or your grandfather's laugh, to someone who never heard it. You'll get a few words in: warm, a bit low, it cracks at the end. And then you'll stop, because the words are so much smaller than the thing. It isn't that you don't know it. You know it better than almost anything. It's that knowing and telling are different skills, and some things only allow one of them. Parents trying to describe the first moment they held their child hit the same wall. Pauri 37 climbs to the very top of the Japji's ladder, and at the end of it, Guru Nanak hits that wall too, and says so.
screen: `DESCRIBE A VOICE YOU LOVE.` → `THE WORDS ARE TOO SMALL.` → `KNOWING ISN'T TELLING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: in the realm of grace, the language is power, and there is no one else. Who lives there? Tithai jodh mahaabal soor. Warriors of great strength, heroes, and the Lord, here called Raam, a name the Granth uses for the One who fills everything, is completely present in them. They neither die nor are deceived, the stanza says, those in whose minds the One lives. Devotees of many worlds dwell there, full of joy, the True One in their hearts. That's the fourth realm, Karam Khand. Then the fifth, the top of the ladder: sach khandd vasai nirankaar. In the realm of truth dwells the Formless One. Sach Khand. And what does the Formless do there? Kar kar vekhai nadar nihaal. Creating, He watches over it all, and blesses with a glance. You've heard that watching before, in Pauris 30 and 31. Here it's at home. In Sach Khand, the stanza says, there are continents and worlds and universes without end; worlds upon worlds of forms, each moving as the order moves it. He sees, He is delighted, He reflects. And then Nanak stops. Nanak kathnaa karrarraa saar. To describe it is as hard as steel. Saar is steel, iron. You could chew on it forever and not bite through. That's today's line. The highest point of the Japji ends not with a description but with an honest admission. Many Sikhs understand Sach Khand not only as a place after this life but as a state to be touched now, in the heart, when the Formless is near.
screen: `KARAM KHAND — THE MIGHTY IN SPIRIT.` · `SACH KHAND — THE FORMLESS DWELLS.` · `HE WATCHES, BLESSING WITH A GLANCE.` · `KATHNAA KARRARRAA SAAR.` · then, large: `HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and bring to mind the things you're grateful for, one at a time, without describing them. A face. A meal. A morning. A voice. Don't find the words. Just let each one arrive, and feel the thanks, and let it go. If a word does come, fine; let it pass. Keep going quietly, one gift after another, until the bell. When the list runs out, just rest in the thanks itself. The bell holds the time.
Sach Khand. The realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells, creating and watching with a kindly glance. The fifth realm, the top of the ladder, and too hard to tell.
Your line: hard as steel to tell. Today, when you can't find words for something that moves you, let the silence be enough. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Pauri 38, sound: jat paahaaraa
228.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38, the last stanza before the closing salok, uses the tools of a goldsmith's workshop, furnace, anvil and crucible, as a picture of the disciplined life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sach Khand, the realm of truth. Your line was hard as steel to tell. Did something move you past words? Today, the thirty-eighth and last pauri of the Japji. Day two hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `SACH KHAND — HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.`

segments.voice: Walk down an old bazaar in almost any Punjabi town and you'll find the goldsmiths' lane. Tiny shops, open to the street. In each one, someone sits cross-legged on the floor beside a small furnace, blowing on the coals through a pipe until they glow orange. There's a little anvil, a row of hammers, a pair of tongs, and the steady tap, tap, tap of metal being coaxed into shape. The work is slow. Hurry it, and the gold cracks. Guru Nanak's hearers knew these shops as well as you know a coffee shop. In the last pauri of the Japji, he walks you into one. Today, listen to its sounds.
screen: `THE GOLDSMITHS' LANE.` → `A SMALL FURNACE, A LITTLE ANVIL.` → `TAP, TAP, TAP.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of Pauri 38: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Four words, and each one is a piece of the workshop. Jat: self-restraint, holding yourself in check. Paahaaraa: the smith's furnace, the forge. So: let restraint be the furnace. Dheeraj: patience, steadiness. You'll hear the word dheeraj used in Punjabi and Hindi today, when someone tells you to keep calm and wait. Suniaar: the goldsmith. In Punjab today, a jeweler is still called a sunaar. So: let patience be the goldsmith. Now hear the rhythm. Jat, one short hit. Paahaaraa, long and rolling, like breath on the coals. Dheeraj, firm. Suniaar, opening out at the end. It moves like the work itself: a strike, a long breath, a strike, a long breath. Then the next line keeps building the shop: aharan mat, ved hatheeaar. Aharan: the anvil. Mat: understanding, good sense. Ved: here, knowledge. Hatheeaar: tools. Let understanding be the anvil and knowledge the tools. Notice what Nanak is doing. The whole Japji began with Guru Nanak saying that thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. Now, at the very end, he gives you a place to work: not a temple of thought but a workshop of patience. Tomorrow we'll see what gets made in it. Today, hear the tools laid out on the floor, one by one.
screen: `JAT PAAHAARAA — RESTRAINT, THE FURNACE.` · `DHEERAJ SUNIAAR — PATIENCE, THE GOLDSMITH.` · `A STRIKE, A LONG BREATH.` · `AHARAN MAT — UNDERSTANDING, THE ANVIL.` · then, large: `JAT PAAHAARAA.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Let jat be short, like a tap on metal, and paahaaraa long, like a slow breath on coals. Then add the next line once: aharan mat, ved hatheeaar. Afterward, sit and breathe like a goldsmith working the fire: a slow, steady breath out, as if you were gently blowing on coals, and a quiet breath in. No rushing. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 38. The last pauri of the Japji opens in a goldsmith's shop: restraint is the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil.
Your line: jat paahaaraa, restraint is the furnace. Today, when you feel the urge to snap or rush, hold back one breath, and let the heat work. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 228 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 38, MEANING: THE TRUE MINT.`

229.title: Pauri 38, meaning: the true mint
229.hook: let restraint be the furnace, patience the goldsmith, love the crucible; there the Word is minted (Japji 38)
229.tomorrow: The final salok: air, water, earth
229.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38 ends with the Word minted in the true mint, and Sikhs honor the shabad as the Guru, present in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 38. Your line was jat paahaaraa, restraint is the furnace. Did you hold back one breath before snapping or rushing? Today, what the workshop makes. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

Pick up any coin and look at it closely. There's a stamp on it: a face, a date, a design pressed into the metal with enormous force. That stamp is the whole point. A plain disc of metal is just metal. A struck coin is something people will trust, pass from hand to hand, and spend. Counterfeiters have always tried to fake the stamp, and people have always tested coins: ringing them on a counter, weighing them, even biting them. A true coin comes from a true mint. Yesterday we laid out the goldsmith's tools. Today, the last line of the last pauri tells us what's being struck.
screen: `A COIN AND ITS STAMP.` → `TESTING FOR FAKES.` → `A TRUE COIN, A TRUE MINT.`

segments.voice: The workshop so far: restraint is the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil, knowledge the tools. The stanza keeps going. Bhau khalaa: awe is the bellows, the deep reverence that keeps the fire breathing. Agan tap taau: discipline is the fire's heat. Bhaandaa bhaau: love is the crucible, the vessel that holds the molten metal. And into it, amrit, the nectar, is poured. Then the line everything was building toward: gharreeai sabad sachee ttakasaal. In this true mint, the Word is struck. Sabad, sometimes written shabad, is the Word: the Guru's word, the hymns of the Granth, and for Sikhs something more, because the Guru and the shabad are understood as one. That's why Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru. So what does it mean to mint the Word? It means the Word isn't only read or sung. It's stamped into a life, by heat and patience and love, until that life is a coin other people can trust. A true coin from a true mint. And then Nanak adds the line that closes every climb in the Japji: jin kau nadar karam tin kaar. This is the work of those on whom the glance of grace falls. Nanak nadaree nadar nihaal: the Gracious One, with a glance, fills them with joy. The tools are yours to use. The stamp comes by grace. And the word ttakasaal, a mint, is still used today for traditional schools where Sikhs learn to recite Gurbani carefully, as if each word were a coin to be struck true.
screen: `AWE THE BELLOWS, LOVE THE CRUCIBLE.` · `SABAD — THE WORD, THE GURU.` · `STRUCK INTO A LIFE.` · `THE STAMP COMES BY GRACE.` · then, large: `THE WORD IS MINTED.`

segments.voice: Think of one moment today when you'll need patience: a slow line, a child's question for the fifth time, a coworker who takes forever. Picture it clearly. Now picture yourself as the goldsmith at that moment, not rushing the metal, keeping the fire steady. Breathe slowly, like the bellows: a long breath out, a quiet breath in. Let the patience settle into your hands and your jaw. Stay with the steady fire. The bell holds the time.
Sabad. The Word: the Guru's word, and for Sikhs the Guru itself, struck into a life in the true mint of restraint, patience, awe and love.
Your line: the word is minted. Today, be patient once, on purpose, in the moment you pictured, and let it be one coin struck true. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

screen: `DAY 229 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FINAL SALOK: AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

230.title: The final salok: air, water, earth
230.hook: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother; day and night the nurses (Japji, salok)
230.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning, ending with this closing salok, and its first line is often quoted by Sikhs speaking about care for the environment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabad, and your line: the word is minted. Were you patient once, on purpose? That was the last pauri. Today, the short verse that closes the whole Japji. Day two hundred thirty.

Think about the first few minutes of your life. Before you had a name, before you knew anyone's face, three things met you. Air rushed into your lungs, and you cried. Water: you'd been floating in it for months, and someone washed you in it. And then you were laid down, held, on something solid. Air, water, ground. They were there before any teacher, any parent's voice, any word. Every morning since, they've been there again, without being asked. After thirty-eight stanzas of climbing, the Japji doesn't end at the top of the ladder. It ends with one short verse, and it comes all the way back down to these three.
screen: `YOUR FIRST MINUTES.` → `AIR, WATER, GROUND.` → `THE JAPJI COMES BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Japji opened with a short verse, a salok, before the first pauri: aad sach, true in the beginning. And it closes with one more. Here's how it begins: pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, and earth the great mother. Air as Guru is worth a moment. The breath is what carries every word, every hymn, every sound of the Name. Without air, no teaching reaches anyone. Then: divas raat due daaee daaiaa, khelai sagal jagat. Day and night are the two nurses, a woman and a man who care for a child, and in their lap the whole world plays. It's a family picture of creation: parents, nurses, and all of us, children, playing. Then the tone turns serious. Good and bad deeds are read out in the presence of Dharam, the righteous judge. By their own actions, some come near, some stay far. And the last lines: those who remembered the Name have finished their hard work and gone. Nanak says, their faces shine, and many others are set free along with them. So the Japji ends on shining faces, and not alone: others go free with them. Many Sikhs today quote pavan guroo paanee pitaa when they speak about caring for the earth. If the air is your teacher and the earth your mother, you don't treat them like trash. And notice where it leaves you. Not in a far realm, but right here, breathing, drinking, standing on the ground.
screen: `PAVAN GUROO — AIR IS THE GURU.` · `WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, THE TWO NURSES.` · `FACES SHINE, AND OTHERS GO FREE.` · then, large: `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a window or step outside. If not, stay where you are. Breathe in slowly and feel the air come in: that's the Guru, in the salok's picture. Take a sip of water if you have some, and feel it go down. Then press your feet into the floor, into the earth beneath the building. Air, water, earth. Stay with the breath now, in and out, letting the three hold you, the way they did in your first minutes. The bell holds the time.
The final salok. The short verse that closes the Japji: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother, day and night the nurses, and faces that shine.
Your line: air, water, earth. Today, step outside once and breathe, and treat one of the three a little more kindly than usual. Day two hundred thirty.

231.title: Camp 4 close: the whole Japji
231.hook: thirty-eight pauris and two saloks, from sochai soch to the faces that shine
231.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the whole Japji Sahib every morning as the first bani of Nitnem, often from memory; it stands at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, on its first pages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the final salok. Your line was air, water, earth. Did you step outside and breathe? Today, the last day of this camp, and a look back at the whole Japji. Day two hundred thirty-one.

Seventy-four days ago, this camp began with an alphabet. Thirty-five letters, the Guru's own script, and a promise: we'd hear each stanza before we tried to understand it. Then the Mool Mantar, sounded out. Then one word, jap, recite, remember. And then, one pauri at a time, the whole thing. There are people who have recited the Japji every morning for fifty years, and people who've never heard a line of it, and you are now somewhere in between. You've walked it, stanza by stanza, from the first line to the last. That's worth stopping for. Today, one look back over the whole road.
screen: `SEVENTY-FOUR DAYS AGO: AN ALPHABET.` → `ONE PAURI AT A TIME.` → `THE WHOLE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here is the Japji, all of it, in one breath. It opens with the Mool Mantar, Ik Onkar, one Creator, and a salok: aad sach, true in the beginning, true now. Pauri 1: sochai soch, thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there; walk in the hukam, the order. Then the order, holding everything, and haumai, the I, I, that forgets it. The Giver who never tires. The early hours and nadar, the kindly glance. Four stanzas of suniai, listening, and four of mannai, trusting. Asankh, the countless: devotions, fools, names. The ant who remembers. Even hunger counted as a gift. Then the four stanzas for the yogis: contentment for earrings, wisdom for food, the One who sees though unseen, storehouses filled once, for all. Then the ladder: one tongue becoming millions, the steps to the Beloved, no power of our own. And the five realms: Dharam Khand, this earth, a house for right action. Gian Khand, so many worlds. Saram Khand, the workshop where effort shapes the mind. Karam Khand, grace. Sach Khand, where the Formless dwells, hard as steel to tell. The goldsmith's shop where the Word is minted. And the closing salok: air the Guru, water the father, earth the mother, and faces that shine. Thirty-eight pauris and two saloks. From sochai soch to the faces that shine. Next, a new camp: the depths. We'll step back from the Japji to see the whole Guru Granth Sahib: how it's built, whose voices are in it, and its great themes.
screen: `MOOL MANTAR AND AAD SACH.` · `LISTENING, TRUSTING, THE COUNTLESS.` · `THE YOGIS, THE LADDER.` · `FIVE REALMS, AND THE TRUE MINT.` · then, large: `I ACTUALLY READ IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the stanzas come back on their own. You don't need them in order. Maybe it's the ant, or the storehouses, or the goldsmith's furnace, or suniai, by listening. Whatever line surfaces first, let it sit with you, and say it quietly if you remember it. Then let another come. If none comes, simply rest, breathing, in the quiet the Japji leaves behind. The bell holds the time.
Camp 4 close. The whole Japji, thirty-eight pauris and two saloks, walked one stanza at a time, from sochai soch to the faces that shine.
Your line: I actually read it. Today, if you can find the time, listen to the whole Japji once, start to finish, and hear every stanza you now know. Day two hundred thirty-one.
